Stocks finished strong on Friday capping off a week for the books, with the S&P 500 finishing up 0.6% on the day and up 3.6% over the week. Is Novo Nordisk’s ’s losing streak coming to an end? Novo is getting a boost from its Wegovy pill , which has been flying off the pharmacy shelves since it came to market in January. In the first quarter of this year, sales for the drug were nearly twice what Wall Street was penciling in. It’s been the biggest GLP-1 debut by volume ever. According to Novo, the pill has now reached over 5 million total prescriptions and it's only accelerating: it took 12 weeks to reach its first 1 million patients, but its latest 1 million were added in just a month. A big chunk of that has been through its direct-to-consumer platform. “We are more and more ourselves getting surprised [by] how many people are after a pill rather than an injection, frankly,” CEO Mike Doustdar told analysts on August 5. It’s a bright spot in an otherwise gloomy picture for the Danish pharmaceutical company. Novo has increasingly lost ground to its rival , Eli Lilly, in the lucrative injectable weight loss and diabetes drug market, which still accounts for the vast majority of GLP-1 prescriptions. Eli Lilly — despite having the best-selling drug in the world, Mounjaro and Zepbound — has had an underwhelming debut for its weight loss pill, Foundayo. The drug, which came to market in April, brought in $98 million in revenue in the second quarter, less than the $103 million the Street was expecting. While its pill may not be a blockbuster (yet, at least), the company’s next-generation injectable drug, retatrutide, has had impressive results in clinical trials. So impressive many people aren’t even waiting for FDA approval to start taking it. It’s worth noting that all signs suggest the introduction of oral GLP-1 options has expanded the population of patients on these drugs, meaning they likely aren’t taking away sales from injectables already on the market. While Novo was early to the GLP-1 market with Ozempic, it has spent the past year or so living under Lilly’s shadow. The Wegovy pill has certainly changed the vibe for Novo. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which holds both Lilly and Novo, said the biggest question is if Novo will be able to get the pill to as many patients who want it. The company has had issues with manufacturing capacity in the past. “That all comes down to execution though, and Novo has seen headwinds in ramping up scale to compete with their larger peers,” Mulberry said. The pickup truck has fundamentally shifted in American car culture. Once an effective workhorse primarily marketed to businesses and trades for its utility, the trucks have mutated, from hyper-functional, stripped down vehicles to aspirational purchases priced at levels attainable only for the upper middle class, stuffed with sophisticated technology and creature comforts. That’s what people are buying, so that’s what automakers are selling. That said, a growing set of evidence indicates that this auto niche is leaving behind a lot of possible customers. This thesis has been borne out in a number of emerging competitors to the flagship Ford pickup truck, the F-150, including but not limited to: Chinese automobiles, mostly electric, that have been driving circles around American autos overseas. Stateside competition from the likes of Slate Auto , the Jeff Bezos-backed startup that has promised a $25,000 customizable electric pickup, which is premised on the observation that cars are mostly built today for the top 30% of the market , and is instead choosing to target the other 70%. Tesla , which has its own direct competitor in the oversized and expensive status symbol pickup truck segment in the Cybertruck. Ford’s first attempt to address some of these competitors, the F-150 Lightning, missed the mark and led to a $19.5 billion charge in December . Beset on all sides, Ford’s not going to have a lot more chances to win. That’s one reason the company has been preparing the Universal Electric Vehicle platform , which will allow the company to build EVs more efficiently on the same production lines, in a strategic shift that the company describes as essentially turning the assembly line into an “assembly tree.” Ford has announced the first vehicle built on that platform will be its new electric pickup truck, dubbed the Fathom , that will hit the market starting at $28,350. That list price is nearly half the cost of the average US sales price of a new vehicle in June, and is only slightly more expensive than the average used car. This comes at a financial inflection point for the automobile business in general and the EV business in particular. Used EV prices have been increasing in 2026, defying the gravity that usually hangs on used car prices amid high gasoline prices from the Iran war. The sticker shock from high auto prices has had some significant reverberations around the economy as well; the average MSRP of a new vehicle in June 2026 was $51,394 . With interest rates still well above their post-pandemic lows, car loan terms that were once unthinkable — well past the standard four years, stretching even as high as eight years — have become downright common . That’s why the sub-$30,000 price point is so compelling: Ford’s either got to find a way to sell cars to the middle class again, or the likes of China and Slate Auto are going to do it for them. title: 🔓 SpaceX unlocked
body_text: Single chord changes, especially in experimental music, aren’t often much to get too excited about, but yesterday’s addition of an eighth note in a performance of John Cage’s “ORGAN²/ASLSP (As SLow aS Possible)” is a pretty big deal in the pretty narrow world of avant-garde art projects that span six centuries . A single small organ in Germany has now played the same Cage composition for 25 years and is, as of yesterday’s new chord, 4% of the way through the piece, meaning that it should wrap up in just 614 years from now. Apparently the full thing still won’t drag as much as the local school orchestra recital you went to that time. For anyone who’s followed the high drama of the journey that SpaceX has been on since its record-breaking IPO less than two months ago — and it’s been difficult to avoid, if we’re all honest — you may expect to see a little more turbulence yet. Today, up to 911.5 million shares held by SpaceX employees and early investors will be made available for sale, as “ the most talked-about lockup in the history of IPO lockups ,” as one brokerage firm CEO put it, begins to loosen. To provide a little context, the company’s June IPO put roughly 639 million shares out to the public, meaning that this first tranche of unlocked stock would (if literally everyone sold up ) more than double the current market supply. Obviously there’s been a lot of speculation about what the potential flood of new shares could do to SpaceX’s price, which was down more than 20% going into its first ever earnings report on Tuesday, and further subdued coming out the other side. Making things a little more tricky to navigate for insiders and investors alike is the structure of the SpaceX lockup release plan , which Bernstein analyst Douglas Harned noted is an “unusually complex scheme” compared to a traditional 180-day expiry date. This first batch of shares won’t even be the biggest unlock this year; a further 1.3 billion (28% of shares subject to the 180-day lockup period) will be released after the company’s next quarterly earnings release. Almost exactly one year on from the company’s IPO, a whopping 6.4 billion shares of Class A common stock (representing Elon Musk’s total shares in the company) will become available. SpaceX has already had a bumpy ride on the public market so far, and its staggered lockup scheme might only add to that.
